title: Saudi Arabia's Red Sea crude bypass peaks in March and declines 41% by June, Wood Mackenzie data shows
gist: Wood Mackenzie vessel-tracking data shows Middle East Gulf crude exports collapsed 82% between January and June 2026, from 18.8 million b/d across 370 cargoes to about 3.4 million b/d across 71 cargoes, after US-Israel strikes on Iran on 28 February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia's East-West Petroline workaround to Yanbu peaked at roughly 4.07 million b/d in March and has since fallen 41% to about 2.39 million b/d in June, while Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar have gone to zero exports — and analyst Ian Solis warns Yanbu simply swaps Hormuz risk for Bab al-Mandeb risk.

insights.claim: Middle East Gulf crude exports fell 82% between January and June 2026, from an average of 18.8 million barrels per day across 370 cargoes to approximately 3.4 million barrels per day across 71 cargoes.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 15.4 million b/d physical supply hole is the single largest crude dislocation on record — the reference number for sizing any 2026 oil price scenario.
insights.quote: From January to June 2026, crude exports from the Middle East Gulf fell 82%, from an average of 18.8 million barrels per day across 370 cargoes to approximately 3.4 million barrels per day across 71 cargoes
insights.locator: Gulf crude exports fall 82% from January baseline

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz carried approximately 11.4 million barrels per day of crude capacity in January and February 2026, averaging 6.3 large crude carrier movements per day, before traffic effectively ceased following US-Israel strikes on Iran on 28 February.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Fixes the pre-conflict baseline at 11.4 million b/d and 6.3 LCC movements/day — the yardstick for judging how much recovery is priced.
insights.quote: The Strait of Hormuz carried approximately 11.4 million barrels per day of crude capacity in January and February 2026, averaging 6.3 large crude carrier movements per day
insights.locator: The Strait of Hormuz carried approximately 11.4 million barrels

insights.claim: By early July 2026 large crude carrier movements through the Strait of Hormuz had partially recovered to approximately 4.4 vessels per day, still 30% below pre-conflict levels, with Suezmax outbound transits at zero and total transit vessel counts down 97% from pre-conflict norms.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Partial recovery in the largest vessels masks a near-total shutdown of everything else — headline transit counts overstate normalisation.
insights.quote: with Suezmax outbound transits at zero, transit vessel counts down 97% from pre-conflict norms, and freight rates approximately three times pre-conflict levels
insights.locator: By early July, large crude carrier movements had partially recovered

insights.claim: Crude freight rates in the region are running at approximately three times pre-conflict levels as of early July 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Tanker owners with Gulf and Red Sea exposure are the clearest beneficiaries of the dislocation — 3x rates is direct earnings upside for VLCC/product carrier fleets.
insights.locator: By early July, large crude carrier movements had partially recovered

themes.theme: Producers with no bypass have gone to zero

insights.claim: Iraq exported 3.77 million barrels per day of crude in January 2026 and recorded zero exports by June, having no pipeline bypass alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Iraq's 3.77 million b/d going to zero is the largest single-country loss — fiscal and sovereign credit stress there is a second-order consequence to watch.
insights.quote: Iraq, which exported 3.77 million barrels per day in January, recorded zero exports by June.
insights.locator: Iraq, which exported 3.77 million barrels per day

insights.claim: Kuwait's crude exports fell from 1.19 million barrels per day to zero from April 2026, and Qatar's from 0.72 million barrels per day in January to zero from April, both because they are entirely dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for seaborne crude access.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Confirms zero-export status for two more OPEC members — OPEC quota and compliance data is meaningless as a supply signal in this period.
insights.quote: Kuwait fell from 1.19 million barrels per day to zero from April. Qatar, at 0.72 million barrels per day in January, also recorded zero from April.
insights.locator: Iraq, which exported 3.77 million barrels per day

insights.claim: Pipeline bypass capacity, not reserves or production capacity, is what determines which Gulf producers can still export during a Hormuz closure — Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar all lack one and went to zero.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for chokepoint risk: rank producers by evacuation optionality, not by production capacity or reserves.
insights.quote: All three producers are entirely dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for seaborne crude access and have no pipeline bypass alternative.
insights.locator: All three producers are entirely dependent

insights.claim: The UAE maintained a diminished export position of approximately 0.56 million barrels per day in June 2026, accounting for 68.6% of all non-Saudi Gulf exports in the June-July period.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The UAE is now effectively the only non-Saudi Gulf exporter still functioning, concentrating residual Gulf supply risk in a single country.
insights.quote: The UAE maintained a diminished position of approximately 0.56 million barrels per day in June, accounting for 68.6% of all non-Saudi Gulf exports in the June-July period.
insights.locator: The UAE maintained a diminished position

themes.theme: Saudi Yanbu pivot and its decay

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia redirected virtually all crude exports through its East-West Petroline to the Red Sea terminal at Yanbu after the Strait of Hormuz closed in late February 2026, reaching a peak of approximately 4.07 million barrels per day in March.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: 4.07 million b/d is the demonstrated ceiling of Saudi bypass capability — a hard cap on how much Gulf supply can be rescued in any future chokepoint event.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia redirected virtually all crude exports through its East-West Petroline to Yanbu on the Red Sea following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in late February, reaching a peak of approximately 4.07 million barrels per day in March.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia redirected virtually all crude exports

insights.claim: Saudi Yanbu loadings had fallen to approximately 2.39 million barrels per day by June 2026 — a 41% reduction from the March peak and a 66% decline from Saudi Arabia's January total export level of approximately 7.96 million barrels per day across Gulf and Red Sea terminals.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The bypass is not holding — Saudi exports are now a third of January levels, a bullish structural fact the market may be underweighting.
insights.quote: By June, Yanbu loadings had fallen to approximately 2.39 million barrels per day — a 41% reduction from the March peak and a 66% decline from Saudi Arabia's January total export level of approximately 7.96 million barrels per day
insights.locator: Despite the near-total concentration of exports through Yanbu

insights.claim: The share of Saudi liftings originating from Yanbu rose from 86.7% in March 2026 to 93.6% in April, 94.3% in May and 98.6% in June, with only a single cargo of about one million barrels clearing the Gulf at Ju'aymah during June.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Near-total single-terminal concentration means one Yanbu or Red Sea outage now takes out essentially all Saudi seaborne supply.
insights.quote: That concentration rose to 93.6% in April, 94.3% in May and 98.6% in June, with only a single cargo of approximately one million barrels clearing the Gulf at Ju'aymah during the month.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia's Red Sea pivot peaks — then declines

insights.claim: In March 2026 Saudi Arabia lifted 121.9 million barrels across 77 cargoes from Yanbu, representing 86.7% of all Saudi liftings that month.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cargo-count granularity gives a monthly tracking template for spotting whether Saudi volumes are stabilising or continuing to decay.
insights.quote: In March, 86.7% of Saudi liftings originated from Yanbu, representing 121.9 million barrels across 77 cargoes at an average of approximately 4.07 million barrels per day.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia's Red Sea pivot peaks — then declines

insights.claim: Saudi Red Sea crude in June and July 2026 went overwhelmingly to South and East Asian destinations — 11 cargoes to Ain Sukhna in Egypt for onward pipeline movement, five to Malacca, four to Karachi, three each to New Mangalore and Sikka in India, and two each to Ulsan and Yeosu in South Korea and Yokkaichi in Japan.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Asian refiners are absorbing the residual Saudi barrel, so Asian crack spreads and refinery run rates are the place to read the shortage.
insights.locator: The destination profile for Saudi Red Sea crude

insights.claim: No direct European crude deliveries were recorded from Saudi Red Sea terminals during June and July 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: European refiners have been fully displaced from Saudi barrels and must source elsewhere — bullish for Atlantic Basin differentials.
insights.quote: No direct European crude deliveries were recorded from Saudi Red Sea terminals during this period.
insights.locator: The destination profile for Saudi Red Sea crude

insights.claim: Refined product flows from the Middle East Gulf have continued at reduced levels, with 171 MEG-origin product cargoes recorded in June and July 2026 including jet fuel to Pembroke in the UK and Le Havre in France and ULSD to Constantza in Romania.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Products are still reaching Europe even as crude does not — the dislocation is far more severe in crude than in refined product supply.
insights.locator: Refined product flows from the region

insights.claim: Four product cargoes loaded at Jubail on the Saudi Gulf coast in early July 2026, indicating limited commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains possible for smaller vessels.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Small-vessel transits are the leading indicator of a Hormuz reopening — watch Jubail loadings before the headline LCC counts move.
insights.quote: Four product cargoes loaded at Jubail on the Saudi Gulf coast in early July, indicating limited commercial passage for smaller vessels.
insights.locator: Refined product flows from the region

insights.claim: Yanbu is not genuine diversification because it has its own chokepoint — a sustained Houthi naval blockade of Bab al-Mandeb would cut Asia off from a major crude supply artery, according to Wood Mackenzie data analyst Ian Solis.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The market's assumed Hormuz hedge is itself exposed — Bab al-Mandeb headlines are an unpriced second-leg tail risk for crude.
insights.quote: What looked like diversification was in reality a shift from one strategic bottleneck to another.
insights.locator: “For months, the market treated Yanbu as the answer to Hormuz risk,”

insights.claim: The market spent months treating Yanbu as the answer to Hormuz risk, a consensus assumption Wood Mackenzie's own vessel data now contradicts given the 41% decline in Yanbu volumes since March.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A named consensus mispricing — positions premised on the Saudi bypass holding up are exposed to further volume decay.
insights.quote: For months, the market treated Yanbu as the answer to Hormuz risk
insights.locator: “For months, the market treated Yanbu as the answer to Hormuz risk,”
